Russian President Vladimir Putin has promoted the country's own satellite internet project.

Elon Musk is a "real genius", Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Wednesday after revealing the two are in "close" contact about satellite technology.

The remarks came during the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, during which Putin discussed Russia's own satellite internet project Rassvet, which provides internet connections to people from satellites.

"He's a genius, a real genius," Putin said of Musk, according to a translation of his remarks by the BBC. "We are in close contact with our American partners, including Mr. Musk."

Starlink is part of Musk's company SpaceX. The company did not respond to a request for comment.

Putin added that it was important for Russia to be in contact with Musk so Rassvet and Starlink satellites do not "interfere with each other in orbit".

"We and our American partners value this mutually, and despite all the political questions, we are working hard," he said.

Starlink has launched roughly 13,000 of its satellites, according to the company. By contrast there are only a couple of dozen Rassvet satellites currently in orbit, according to online satellite trackers.

The Russian Embassy in South Africa said on Wednesday Rassvet is "Russia's Starlink alternative" and "marks only the country's first steps in this field".

"Russia maintains close contacts with the US on space, including with Elon Musk," the embassy wrote.

Putin's comments about Rassvet and Starlink were made as the US and Russia appear to be growing closer, even as it approaches five years since Putin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Ukraine relied on Starlink internet in its efforts to keep Russia's forces at bay. But its military last week suddenly suffered Starlink connectivity problems, something Musk has admitted SpaceX did intentionally.

US President Donald Trump earlier this month said he'd struck a deal with Russia to import diesel in an effort to lower gas prices that have skyrocketed due to the US war with Iran.

Then Trump waived certain sanctions against Russia that were set to take effect.

Not long after, a US citizen was released from Russian custody, with US envoy Steve Witkoff referring to Putin as a "humanitarian".

Musk was born in South Africa and then immigrated to Canada before settling in the US. All of his business ventures, including Tesla, SpaceX and Starlink, are based in America, with most operating out of California and Texas.

The billionaire, and off and on again trillionaire, has been one of the biggest political allies and financiers of Trump and other Republican US politicians.

Umuramyi Yves Rwagasore yashyize hanze indirimbo nshya yise “Nizeye”, avuga ko ishingiye ku buhamya bw’ibyo Imana yamukoreye mu myaka ishize, birimo gusohoza amasezerano yari yaramuhaye.

Uyu muhanzi ukorera umurimo wo kuramya no guhimbaza Imana muri Canada, yavuze ko iyi ndirimbo yagiye hanze ku wa 23 Ukwakira 2026, yayanditse agaruka ku bihe yanyuzemo, aho hari ibyo yabonaga ko bigoye kugeraho ariko nyuma akabona Imana ibimufashamo.

Ati ‘Nizeye’ yaje mu buryo bw’ubuhamya. Ni indirimbo nanditse nshingiye ku byo Imana yankoreye. Nyuma y’imyaka myinshi, uwabibara ntiyabishobora. Hari ibyo nabonaga bigoye ariko Imana ikabikuraho, amasezerano menshi yarasohoye, andi na yo nizeye ko azasohora.”

Yasobanuye ko yahisemo kuyita “Nizeye” kugira ngo agaragaze akamaro ko gukomeza kugira ibyiringiro, nubwo hari ibyo umuntu aba agitegereje.

Yagize ati “Izina ‘Nizeye’ rifite igisobanuro gikomeye mu buzima bwanjye; ko nkwiriye kubaho nizeye Imana kuko ntishidikanywaho, ikora icyo yavuze kandi ntishobora kwivuguruza. Ndufuza ko ubutumwa bwayo bwafasha abacitse intege kongera kugira imbaraga zo gukomeza urugendo rwabo.”

Yves Rwagasore ni umwe mu baramyi nyarwanda bazwi mu ndirimbo zirimo “Njyewe Yesu Yankunze”, “Wowe Ntujya Uhemuka”, “Abiringiye Uwiteka”, “Thank You God”, “Narababariwe”, “Intsinzi”, “Asante”, “Uniongoze”, “Aranziyesu Uriho”, “Urakwiye”, “Hari Ikintu Kimwe” na “Teach Me Your Way”.

Uyu muramyi avuga ko ageze kure atuganya indirimo zizaba ziri kuri ‘Album ’ yise Ndakomeje.

MN202610_8d0wxwtteq.t:
Amazon Prime Air is expanding to 500 US towns and cities

Nature lover Ashley Schmidt no longer spends much time in her garden, in the Dallas suburb of North Garland.

She's also given up on cycling to the local parks where she previously enjoyed taking close-up photos of the bugs, lizards and toads.

It's all because she can't stand the sound of the delivery drones that fly overhead, depositing her neighbours' online orders.

"They emit this very annoying buzz. It triggers my fight or flight response," says the 44-year-old administrative assistant.

"You can hear the drones on approach and you can hear them inside your home when they pass directly overhead and then you hear them as they leave," she says.

Amazon says it is working to reduce the noise of its drone fleet

Schmidt is one of a growing number of people living with the noise of drones dispatched by companies including Amazon and Walmart as they seek to speed up home deliveries.

Delivery drone services, not long ago a novelty, are becoming part of everyday life for many people in the US.

Among them, Amazon Prime Air is in the process of expanding deliveries to nearly 500 cities and towns, delivering items that fit into a space the size of a shoe box. It has also launched to customers in and around Darlington in the north of England.

Smaller drone delivery services are popping up too: in some US cities, customers can order flying treats from their local pizza joint or ice cream parlour.

Even in cities where noise is already a steady part of life, the sound of drones seems to irk in a particular way.

While the steady passing of traffic might blend into the background, the sudden whine of a drone's rotors can pierce the everyday hum.

The sound tends to be "particularly noticeable, even when overall sound levels are relatively low," says Antonio Torija Martinez, professor in acoustic engineering and psychoacoustics at the University of Salford.

Unlike planes, drones operate at low altitudes and may fly directly over residential areas.

"They can expose communities that have not previously experienced significant aircraft noise, and who may therefore be more sensitive to changes in their local soundscape," says Torija Martinez.

He points to research showing that people respond strongly to a noise when they consider the source to be "novel, intrusive or frequent". People who benefit from a drone delivery service, for example, may be less bothered by the noise.

However, complaints about the sound of drones are likely to grow, he warns: "At the moment we are seeing some of these problems localised in some areas, but… as the drone sector expands, more and more of these complaints will happen."

In the US, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) regulates commercial drones, but it has come under fire for allowing noisy drone delivery operations. The FAA says operators and local community leaders have primary responsibility for addressing any community concerns.

Greenjets encloses some of the blades on its drone inside a pod

Might better technology muffle the irritating buzz?

One startup, Greenjets, set out to tackle both "noise level and the frequency of that noise," as Darren James, future technologies lead at the company, puts it.

The London-based business has designed a propulsion system it claims can reduce drone noise by at least two thirds.

While standard drones use spinning propellers that slice through open air, creating that high-pitched buzz, Greenjets encloses spinning blades inside a pod, to muffle the sound and direct the noise away from the ground.

Its system also quietens things down through slower rotor speed and by using materials that reduce vibration noise.

Making quieter drones isn't just about keeping the noise down for neighbours who are already sick of airborne deliveries.

Greenjets' low-noise tech has been used by police and harbour security teams in Germany. It has also helped conservationists in Africa, who are seeking to track poachers from above without being detected.

Battlefield drone operators also have good reason to keep the noise down, to avoid alerting the enemy of the approach of their unmanned vehicles.

"There are some efforts to reduce the sound of drones. The US Special Forces are interested, at an experimental stage," says Robert Tollast, a research fellow at Whitehall think tank The Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).

But he stresses that drone speed, rather than stealthiness, tends to come first for larger drones used in the war between Russia and Ukraine. "Make it faster, not less quiet, seems to be the approach," says Tollast.

Sharrow Engineering developed twisted propellers that reduce noise

For Detroit-based entrepreneur, Greg Sharrow, it was the challenge of broadcasting a classical music performance back in 2012 that set him on the path to quieter drone design.

He needed to film a violinist from a tricky angle and a drone seemed the only solution – except that it would be far too noisy.

As a starting point, "I knew that most of the noise from the drone was coming from the propeller, not the motor," he says. Specifically, it was the tips of the blades that he realised were creating the noise as they swiped through the air.

"I asked myself a very simple question, what would a tipless propeller look like and how would it function?"

The result was to create a propeller with twisted loop-shaped blades with no points.

It turned out it was easier to test his propeller in water than it was to repeatedly fly a drone, which led Sharrow to initially develop a less noisy boat propeller. Now, however, his company, Sharrow Engineering, is focusing on developing "ultra-quiet" drone rotors.

"We have validated that the technology works in drone applications and that it is dramatically quieter," says Sharrow.

Companies at the forefront of drone deliveries say they are also working to reduce the noise of their fleets. A spokesperson for Amazon says it has made "measurable sound improvements" to its drones and its latest designs use custom-designed propellers "that produce almost half the perceived sound of the prior generation, with a milder tone".

Drone maker Wing, which provides its vehicles for Walmart deliveries, says its propellers are designed to minimise noise. It also varies its flight paths to prevent repeated overflights over any single home or neighbourhood.

For Schmidt, fed up with the noise of drones, the only truly satisfactory solution would be to halt drone deliveries in her area. "I would like them to completely stop until they figure out how their services stop being a nuisance," she says.

MN202610_1j5m5vkf2ce.t:
Umutwe w'inyeshyamba wa FRN urwanya ubutegetsi bwa Repubulika ya Demokarasi ya Congo (DRC) watangaje ko uwari umusirikare wo ku rwego rwa jenerali mu ngabo z'icyo gihugu (FARDC) yazivuyemo akawusanga ngo bakorane.

Itangazo ry'umuvugizi wa FRN Lawrence Kanyuka rivuga ko Général de Brigade François Kamanzi yari umukuru w'ibikorwa mu karere ka 12 ka gisirikare mu ngabo za DRC ko mu ntara ya Kongo-Central.

Kanyuka yongeyeho ko abandi basirikare bakuru babiri na bo bahisemo kwifatanya na FRN ndetse ko mu minsi iri imbere izatangaza imyirondoro yabo.

Umwe mu basirikare bakuru ba FARDC yabwiye BBC Gahuzamiryango mu butumwa bwanditse ati: "Bibaye ari uko bimeze, byaba biteye isoni ku mwuga wacu wa gisirikare."

BBC Gahuzamiryango yanagerageje kuvugana n'umuvugizi wa FARDC.

Kanyuka yavuze ko Kamanzi "yahisemo kwitandukanya n'ubutegetsi bwa Kinshasa, bugaba ibitero buri munsi ku bushake ku baturage b'abasivile". Ntibisobanutse uburyo n'igihe Kamanzi yagereye muri FRN.

Impande zombi ziri muri iyi ntambara – imaze imyaka hafi itanu yongeye kubura mu burasirazuba bw'igihugu – zishinjwa kugaba ibitero by'indege nto z'intambara zitajyamo umupilote (drone) mu bice bituwemo n'abasivile.

FRN yabitangaje ku wa kabiri nijoro nyuma y'amasaha ibiro bya Perezida wa DRC Félix Tshisekedi bitangaje videwo imugaragaza ubwo yari ari mu nama n'abadepite n'abasenateri mu cyumweru gishize, avuga ko igihe cyose azaba agifite "igitonyanga cy'amaraso mu mubiri" we azakomeza kurwanirira igihugu cye.

Muri iryo jambo, rya mbere yari avuze ku mugaragaro kuva uwo yasimbuye ku butegetsi Joseph Kabila atangajwe nk'umukuru wa FRN mu byumweru bibiri bishize, Tshisekedi yavuze ko ibyabaye byemeje ibyo yari yaravuze ko Kabila ari we wari uri inyuma ya M23.

Yongeyeho ati: "Mu bya gisirikare, jyewe mfitiye icyizere ingabo zacu nubwo twagize ibibazo byinshi bivuye ku bacengezi n'abagambanyi. Simvuze ko bose twabaranduye ariko muri iki gihe twashoboye kubatera ubwoba. Uyu munsi, niba hakiri abagambanyi, ntibagikora ku mugaragaro nkuko byari bimeze mu gihe gito gishize."

Raporo yo mu 2017 y'umuryango uharanira uburenganzira bwa muntu Human Rights Watch ivuga ko François Kamanzi yahoze mu wari umutwe w'inyeshyamba wa RCD warwanyije ubutegetsi bwa Laurent-Désiré Kabila – se wa Joseph Kabila – nyuma yuko ashwanye n'abamufashije mu mutwe wa AFDL, barimo u Rwanda, mu guhirika ubutegetsi bwa Mobutu Sese Seko.

Bamwe mu bari bagize RCD nyuma baje gushinga umutwe w'inyeshyamba wa CNDP wari uyobowe na Laurent Nkunda. Bamwe mu bari bari muri CNDP ni bo baje gushinga M23, ubu yahindutse FRN.

Uwavuganye na BBC Gahuzamiryango ukurikiranira hafi ibibera mu karere k'ibiyaga bigari avuga ko Kamanzi yakoranye na Nkunda by'igihe gito ariko aza gutandukana na we ubwo benshi bari batangiye kuva muri CNDP.

Ku butegetsi bwa Joseph Kabila, wategetse DRC imyaka 18 kuva mu 2001 kugeza muri Mutarama (1) mu 2019, Kabila yagize Kamanzi umukuru wungirije w'akarere ka gisirikare ushinzwe ibikorwa n'iperereza mu ntara ya Kivu ya Ruguru, mu burasirazuba bw'igihugu.

Amakuru avuga ko Kamanzi, uvuka muri teritwari ya Rutshuru, yarwanye mu zari inyeshyamba za RPA/RPF zaje gufata ubutegetsi mu Rwanda mu 1994, nyuma y'urugamba rwiswe urwo kubohora igihugu rwatangiye mu Kwakira (10) mu 1990.

Raporo z'inzobere za ONU zishinja u Rwanda gufasha uwari umutwe wa M23. U Rwanda rurabihakana.

Ukujya muri FRN kwa Kamanzi gutangajwe mu gihe amakuru avuga ko imirwano ikaze imaze igihe yongeye kubura mu ntara ya Kivu y'Epfo muri teritwari ya Uvira.

Mu Kuboza (12) mu 2025, umujyi wa Uvira wari wafashwe by'igihe gito n'uwari umutwe w'inyeshyamba wa AFC/M23, uza kuwuvamo ku gitutu cy'amahanga arangajwe imbere n'Amerika.

Ku wa kabiri, Amerika yatangaje ko intumwa zikora igenamigambi rya gisirikare z'u Rwanda na DRC zahuriye mu nama i Garmisch mu Budage, muri gahunda yo gushyira mu ngiro amasezerano y'amahoro Perezida Tshisekedi na Perezida w'u Rwanda Paul Kagame basinye mu Kuboza (12) mu 2025, yahagarikiwe na Perezida w'Amerika Donald Trump.

Iyo nama ikurikiye iya gatandatu yabereye i Genève mu Busuwisi muri Kanama (8), Amerika ivuga ko yari iyo kunoza umushinga w'ibikorwa mbere yuko wemezwa, ujyanye n'ibyo impande zombi ziyemeje mu by'umutekano mu masezerano ya Washington.

DRC yiyemeje kurandura/kubuza gukora ("neutralisation") umutwe w'inyeshyamba wa FDLR urwanya ubutegetsi bw'u Rwanda ukorera mu burasirazuba bwa DRC, naho u Rwanda rwiyemeza gukura ingabo mu bikorwa ("disengagement of forces") no gukuraho "ingamba z'ubwirinzi".

MN202610_1lm99lb16zx.t:
Arno Yafunga Botay is one of six athletes competing for the Refugee Olympic Team at the Dakar 2026 Youth Games

Arno Yafunga Botay was six when his family fled the Democratic Republic of Congo after threats to his father's life culminated in an attack on their home which claimed the life of his seven-month-old sibling.

Following a spell living in the Kakuma refugee camp in north-west Kenya, the family settled in Nairobi. There, Arno used to watch his father Arnold practising judo and eventually asked him to teach him the sport.

Now, having coming through trials in East Africa , he will compete for the Refugee Olympic Team in the under-55kg category at the Dakar 2026 Youth Games.

"I didn't expect to be selected," the 15-year-old told BBC Sport Africa.

"I was so excited. I was crying tears of joy."

This is the first time that a team of refugees will appear at a Youth Games.

"It [means] a lot to me to represent other refugees, represent my community," Yafunga Botay added.

The family have been in Kenya since they were forced to leave DR Congo in 2017.

"There were people who wanted to kill me," Arnold said.

"At the time, I was detained somewhere when people came to our house and attacked my family. The situation led to the death of my child."

All you need to know about the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympics

Africa prepares for historic Olympic moment at Dakar 2026

After finding safety, Yafunga Botay and his elder brother Christian would watch their father training before he headed out to work as a labourer.

Yafunga Botay began receiving instructions in judo rules and techniques at the age of seven.

However, life in their adopted East African nation provided its own challenges.

"I [did] not have the judogi clothes or transport fees for local competitions," he explained.

"It's been difficult going to school. There's no money for school fees.

"My father has no work. He needs to go to work and give us money to go and pay the school fees.

"And here we don't have support. As a refugee, to stay in Kenya, you need to have documents.

"[Thankfully] the IOC (International Olympic Committee) came with this programme of helping refugees achieve their dreams."

The Refugee Olympic Team have been mentored by marathon great Eliud Kipchoge (back row, second from right)

The Refugee Olympic Team was first introduced at the Rio 2016 Olympics and Cameroon-born boxer Cindy Ngamba won the team's first ever medal at Paris 2024 when she claimed bronze in the women's 75kg category .

In a double first, the team will now make its Youth Olympics debut at Dakar 2026, which is the first Olympic event hosted on African soil.

"As a refugee, we have a right to compete," Yafunga Botay said.

"A refugee is a human being like other people."

Father Arnold says the team serves as a message of hope to people around the world who have been displaced.

"Being a refugee does not mean your life is over," he said.

"Refugees can also do things that surprise people.

"My message to fellow refugees is don't give up. Keep pushing until the end."

The six-strong team competing in Senegal is being mentored by two-time Olympic marathon champion Eliud Kipchoge.

"He teaches us [to] respect the coach, focus on what you are doing," Yafunga Botay said.

"I promised him I'll bring the gold medal [back] so he can see [what] I achieved."

Arnold takes a hands-on approach to coaching Arno, grappling with his son in their Nairobi dojo

Judo has become a central part of life for the family.

Arnold still coaches Yafunga Botay and Christian, now 17, occasionally serves as his younger brother's sparring partner.

The teenager describes his father as "strict" even at home, with a firm focus on the importance of discipline.

"Maintaining his weight is not easy. He [Arno] has to keep training consistently," Arnold said.

"Judo teaches him respect and helps him interact with others, whether at school or at home.

"Those lessons follow him everywhere. In judo, every time you fall you gain the strength to keep going."

The owner of the dojo in the Kenyan capital where Yafunga Botay has trained since 2020 says his selection for Dakar 2026 has "changed perceptions" of judo in the community.

"It is helping parents understand that judo is not just a fighting sport - it has real value," Lawrence Karisa Nyundo told the BBC.

"I have received calls from parents who want to enrol their children.

"It is a big achievement for this club that one of our athletes is going to compete at the Olympics. We are praying that he performs well."

After Dakar, Yafunga Botay hopes other refugees can benefit from his experience in the future.

"I think if I achieve [a] gold medal, I can go there and teach them the value of judo."

Competition at Dakar 2026 begins on Friday, with the opening ceremony a day later and judo events running from 1-3 November.

MN202610_1k96sg8u1eu.t:
Paul Stirling had half-centuries in both of his innings in the Namibia series

Ireland captain Paul Stirling will miss the final two games of his side's one-day international series in Namibia after fracturing his finger.

The 36-year-old sustained the injury while fielding during his side's loss in the third ODI on Tuesday, a result that leaves his side trailing their hosts 2-1 in the five-match series.

Tim Tector, brother of middle-order batter Harry Tector, has been called up as a replacement.

The younger Tector sibling is uncapped in ODIs, although he has made eight appearances for the side in T20 cricket, averaging 17 in the shorter format.

Battling to save the series, the injury to Stirling is another blow to head coach Gary Wilson.

The Ireland opener was unable to bat in his side's innings following the injury on Tuesday, but had a pair of half-centuries in the first two games in Windhoek, leading the side with scores of 56 and 77.

Ireland won the opener of the series on 22 October but have suffered losses of 31 and 63 runs in the two games since.

The series, which is being used by Ireland as preparation for next year's World Cup qualifiers, resumes on Friday before a concluding fixture on Sunday.
